note: Week 1 lessons. Written to give each day plain-language context before the resources. resourceId links to a resource id in the resource packs. lookFor (version 2) says what a good answer to each check-yourself question includes; it is written from the lesson's own key ideas and words.

lessons.title: Get your lab ready
lessons.inOneSentence: Set up Docker so you can run a real identity system on your own laptop.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Identity products are configured by admins, not only designed. Running a real admin console shows you what those admins face.
keyIdeas: Docker runs software in an isolated box called a container, so you can start it, break it and delete it cleanly.
Keycloak is an open-source identity provider: the system that signs people in and says who they are.
Nothing this week needs real coding. You will mostly copy commands and click through an admin console.

words.meaning: A running, isolated copy of a program.
The packaged recipe a container is started from.
The system that checks who you are and tells other apps.
Your own list of new words, in your own sentences.

steps.text: Check Docker works: run the version command, then the hello-world test.
Read the Keycloak getting-started page through once. Do not run it yet.
Start your glossary with 10 words you already half-know (login, password, session...) and write each in one sentence.
Spare time: note anything that failed, so you can fix it before Day 3.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not install anything beyond Docker today.
checkYourself: What is the difference between an image and a container?
What does an identity provider do?
lookFor: An image is the packaged recipe; a container is a running, isolated copy started from it. One image can start many containers, and deleting a container leaves the image in place.
It checks who someone is (it signs them in) and then tells other apps who that person is, so each app does not have to handle passwords itself.

lessons.title: Authentication, authorization and accounting
lessons.inOneSentence: Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and accounting records what you did.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Almost every identity screen (login, permissions, audit log) belongs to one of these three. Mixing them up produces confusing products and unsafe defaults.
keyIdeas: Authentication (authN): proving you are who you claim to be, with something you know, have or are.
Authorization (authZ): after you are known, deciding what you are allowed to do. You can be signed in and still be denied.
Accounting: keeping a record of what happened, for investigation and audit.
After you sign in, a session or token stands in for you for a while, so you do not sign in on every click.

words.meaning: What proves your identity, such as a password or passkey.
The period during which the system treats you as signed in.
A small piece of data that represents a session or a permission.
One way of proving identity: something you know, have or are.
A named bundle of permissions.

steps.text: Watch the Messer videos on identity and access. Take notes under three headings: authentication, authorization, accounting.
Write one sentence for each of the three in your own words, with one example from a product you use.
Add the new words to your glossary.

lessons.skipOrSkim: These videos are exam prep. Ignore exam tips and acronym lists you do not need yet.
checkYourself: A user signs in but sees 'access denied' on one page. Which of the three is that?
Give one example of accounting in a product you use.
lookFor: Authorization. Authentication worked (the user is signed in and known), but they are not allowed to see that page. Being signed in and being allowed are different checks.
Any record of who did what and when that you can look back at: for example a 'recent sign-ins' or login-activity list, a document's version history, or an admin audit log.

lessons.title: Your first identity system
lessons.inOneSentence: Run Keycloak and create a small company: a realm, a few users, groups and roles.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is the kind of console real IT admins work in every day. You will design for them, so you should see what it feels like.
keyIdeas: A realm is an isolated space for one organization's users and settings.
A group is who you are with (a team). A role is what you may do. Giving roles to groups scales better than giving them to people one by one.
Each thing you create shows what an admin must understand: the console's words are the admin's vocabulary.

words.meaning: An isolated space for one organization's users and settings.
A set of users, usually a team.
An application that uses Keycloak to sign people in.
The screen where an admin manages users and settings.

steps.text: Start Keycloak with Docker and sign in to the admin console.
Do Exercise 1: create a realm, five users, two groups and two roles, then give a role to a group.
Only when you meet an unfamiliar word, look it up in the administration guide.
Write down three things that surprised you as a designer. They feed Saturday's write-up.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not read the administration guide from the top.
checkYourself: Why give a role to a group rather than to each user?
What is the difference between a realm and a user?
lookFor: People join, move and leave teams. If the role belongs to the group, one change of group membership updates their access, everyone on a team gets the same access, and reviewing access means checking a few groups instead of every person.
A realm is the whole isolated space for one organization: its users, groups, roles and settings. A user is one account inside a realm.

lessons.title: The life of an account, and thinking like an attacker
lessons.inOneSentence: Accounts are created, changed and removed over time, and threat modelling is asking what could go wrong with them.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Many identity failures are lifecycle failures: someone leaves and keeps access. Designing the leaver path well is a real product opportunity.
keyIdeas: Joiner, mover, leaver: people start, change roles and leave. Each change should change their access.
Orphaned accounts and privilege creep (collecting access over time) are the usual problems.
Threat modelling asks four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good job?

words.meaning: The three lifecycle events for a person at an organization.
An account that stays active after its owner has gone.
Slowly collecting more access than you need.
Something that could go wrong, caused on purpose or not.
What you do to reduce a threat.

steps.text: Read the Threat Modeling Manifesto.
Read the beginner's guide to threat modelling.
Apply the four questions to your Day 3 lab. Write three things that could go wrong when someone leaves.
Add the new words to your glossary.

lessons.skipOrSkim: The Manifesto is short and abstract; it will make more sense after the lab.
checkYourself: What is an orphaned account and why does it matter?
Which of the four questions did you find hardest to answer for your lab?
lookFor: An account that stays active after its owner has gone (left, or no longer needs it). It matters because nobody is watching it but it still works, so a former employee or an attacker can use it without anyone noticing.

There is no single right answer. A useful answer names the question, says what made it hard (for example, not yet knowing what can go wrong in an identity system) and notes what you would need to learn or try to answer it better.

lessons.title: Build day: practice data for Project 1
lessons.inOneSentence: Create realistic fake people and apps so you have something to review later.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: You cannot design an access review without messy data. Seed data is how you test whether the tool finds the problems you planted.
keyIdeas: Seed data is fake data made on purpose: here about 50 users and 8 apps (as groups).
Planted stale accounts are test cases with known answers: you decide which ones are stale, so you can check the tool finds them.

words.meaning: A small program that creates test data.
An account that is no longer used or no longer needed.
A file listing which accounts you planted.

steps.text: Write or generate a seed script for 50 users and 8 groups in Keycloak.
Plant several stale accounts and record them in a separate answer-key file.
Read the code and write a comment on what each part does. If an AI tool wrote it, say so in the README.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not build any screens today.
checkYourself: Could you explain every part of the script to an interviewer?
lookFor: Answer honestly, part by part: what does it do and why is it there? Any part you cannot explain yet is the thing to review next, before you show the script to anyone.
You planted the stale accounts on purpose, so you know the right answer. Comparing what the tool finds with the key shows what it caught, what it missed and what it flagged by mistake.

lessons.title: Write it up
lessons.inOneSentence: Turn the week into one piece you share: a README and a one-page diagram of who holds which credential.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Evidence is what makes the learning visible. A clear diagram is also a design deliverable.
keyIdeas: A credential diagram answers: who or what holds which secret, and where does it travel?
Looking at how real admin guides start shows what vendors think an admin must do first.

words.meaning: The first file anyone reads in a project.
What proves identity, such as a password, key or token.

steps.text: Read two admin getting-started guides and list what an admin must do on day one. Do the third only if you have time.
Draw the one-page 'who holds which credential' diagram for your lab.
Write the identity-lab README and share it (for example on GitHub). Add it to Career → Portfolio and mark it as shared.
Optional design exercise: sketch a one-page mental model of an enterprise identity system.

lessons.skipOrSkim: The 1Password and Okta guides have no verified link: search for them, or skip one.
checkYourself: What does an admin need to do on day one in each product?
Which credential in your lab is the riskiest, and why?
lookFor: This depends on your reading. A good answer lists, for each product, the first few things its admin guide asks for and points out what all three have in common and where one differs.

There is no single right answer. A strong answer names one credential (for example the Keycloak admin password or an app's client secret), says who or what holds it and where it travels, and says what someone could do with it if it leaked.
